background.definition: Stevens Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) are rare but life threatening cutaneous immunologically mediated drug reactions, with multi organ involvement. Distinct from erythema multiforme, these acute skin reactions are characterized by sheet-like skin and mucosal loss. SJS and TEN are clinically similar except for their distribution. Lesions affect < 10% of body surface area in SJS and > 30% of body surface ares in TEN. Involvement of 10% to 30% of body surface area is considered a SJS/TEN overlap.

list.listitem: The incidence of Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis combined is 7.4 per 1,000,000 per year.
Stevens-Johnson is three times more common than toxic epidermal necrolysis.
More than half of the cases of the syndrome are thought to involve a drug-related reaction.

Drugs that most commonly cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis are : allopurinol, anticonvulsants (lamotrigine, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbitomne), sulfonamides, antibiotics including minocycline, anti-tuberulcosis and anti-HIV drugs, and NSAIDs. Sulfonamides were the most common cause in one systematic review.

A systematic review of case reports identified 25 reports of 27 patients with macrolide associated SJS or toxic epidemal necrolysis, with 1 death. Time from medication use to onset of symptoms ranged from 1 to 14 days.
In children, medicines used for colds are a common trigger and in certain HLA subgroups are at heightened risk for severe ocular complications.
The relative risk per 10,000 new users is 1.4 for carbamazepine, 2.5 for lamotrigine, 8.1 for phenobarbital, 6.9 for phenytoin, and 0.4 for valproic acid.
Infections (mycoplasma pneumonia, herpes simplex, influenza, coxsackie virus, and others) may also trigger Stevens–Johnson syndrome, especially in children.
In many cases, no triggering drug or infection is identified.
Affected patients may have a genetic predisposition.
Cytotoxic T cells activated by the imposing antigen may express the skin cell receptor.
There is increased expression of cytokines at the epidermis, which may explain the prodromal symptoms.
Keratinocyte apoptosis mediated through Fas and FasL receptors.
The following HLA alleles are associated with sulfamethoxazole/cotrimoxazole induced severe cutaneous adverse reactions: HLA-A*11:01, HLA-B*13:01, HLA-B*15:02, HLA-B*38:02, and HLA-C*0801.
Stevens–Johnson syndrome usually follows drug ingestion and is characterized by prodromal fever and development of target lesions.
At least 2 mucosal surfaces are involved with Stevens–Johnson syndrome.
If more than 20% of the patient's body is involved, diagnose toxic epidermal necrolysis.

Differential.Differential_Features: Less than 10% of body surface area involvement, typically only oral mucosal lesions, and zero or 1 mucous membrane involvement
Not typically associated with drug exposure and active staph infection
No mucosal involvement, nonpainful lesions, typically caused by beta-lactam antibiotics
Rash and mucositis associated with mycoplasma pneumonia, occuring typically i young patients. Commonly oral, ocular, and urogential mucositis.

list.listitem: The patient will have a prodromal fever usually following infection or recent drug ingestion. The fever may be accompanied by cough, sore throat, or headache.

This is followed by acute development of target lesions, which are typically 3-ring target lesions with the outermost ring being the darkest. The rash usually initially appears on the face or chest; ask about the date of appearance.
Inquire about symptoms that indicate involvement of the respiratory tract (cough, dyspnea, hemoptysis), urinary tract (pain, urinary retention), or GI tract (diarrhea, abdominal distension).
Lesions will cover more than 10% but less than 30% of the body surface area in Stevens–Johnson syndrome. More widespread involvement signals toxic epidermal necrolysis.

Identify mucous membrane involvement through a review of symptoms (e.g., shortness of breath involving respiratory mucosa, dysphagia, diarrhea, or abdominal pain involving gastric mucosa, and dysuria involving urinary mucosa) or through physical examination finds of mucosal involvement of the eyes, oral cavity, anus, and urethra.

Take a careful history of drug exposure or recent infections. HSV, mycoplasma, and chlamydia are common triggering infections. Immediately discontinue any potentially offending medications. Exclude staph scalded skin syndrome by inspecting the mucosa, which are not involved in SSSS.
Skin biopsy may provide definitive diagnosis but is not necessary before starting treatment.
Elevated procalcitonin suggests systemic bacterial infection. IT was 85% sensitive and 90% specific in one small poorly described trial.

British guidelines recommend full blood count, CRP, metabolic profile, lactate, and screening for potentially triggering infections such as chlamycia, mycoplasma, HSV, and varicella. They also recommend bacterial swabs from lesions for culture and sensitivity, conjunctival swabs for adenovirus, chlamydia, and HSV. Photographs are suggested to document the extent of lesions.
Patients present with prodromal fever followed by the development of skin lesions and involvement of at least 2 mucous membranes.
Involvement of more than 20% of body surface area signals toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Use SCORTEN score for prognosis ().
Discontinue suspected or known causative agent. C
Supportive care, including topical antiseptics and anesthetics, is important. C
Corticosteroids and cyclosporine may improve survival; there was no benefit seen for thalidomide, cyclophosphamide, tumor necrossis factor inhibitors, or other therapies in a systematic review.B

Mucosal membrane involvement causing pain may be alleviated by viscous lidocaine mixed with petrolatum and applied twice a day. Viscous lidocaine is commonly prepared as 2% lidocaine solution (2% = 20 mg/mL). This solution is suitable for mucous membrane application, but no more than 3 mg per kg per dose every 2 to 3 hours, with a maximum of 8 applications per 24-hour period to prevent systemic toxicity.

To care for dermal involvement, use topical antiseptics such as 0.5% silver nitrate or 0.05% chlorhexidine to paint the area and apply a moist dressing daily. Epidermal debridement and application of biologic skin cover should only be performed and supervised by a wound care specialist.

A systematic review of 96 RCTs of immunomodulating treatments for Stevens-Johnson syndrome found some evidence that glucocorticoids (OR 0.7, 95% CI 0.5-0.97) and cyclosproine (OR 0.1, 95% CI 0.0-0.4) were promising therapies for reducing mortality. This was also the conclusion of a network meta-analysis that included RCTs and observational studies of treatment of toxic epidermal necrolysis. However, while not precluding their use, the British guidelines found no clear evidence for or against use of glucocorticoids, anti-tumour necrosis factor, monoclonal antibodies, or cyclosporin.
Treat secondary infection with antiviral or antibacterial agents.

IVIG infusion at high doses (4 mg/kg) is controversial since it has not been studied in any RCTs. A review of case reports and case series could find no clear evidence of harm or benefit, and they were not recommended by British guidelines.

A Japanese propensity score matched observational study found no difference in mortality for patients treated with IVIG versus plasmapheresis following failure of corticosteroid therapy. Length of stay and cost were higher for those treated with plasmapheresis.
Provide adequate pain control.
Amniotic membrane transfer has been successful in a case series of 10 patients with severe ocular involvement.
Debride any necrotic or infected tissue under anesthesia in a specialized center. Clean debrided wounds using topical antimicrobials, also under anesthesia.
Evaluate and ensure patency of the airway, and if necessary insert a catheter if urinary retention or dysuria.
Stopping the presumptive causative agent is key.
Ensure adequate hydration orally if possible and/or by IV, and monitor the fluid balance; there are significant fluid losses, particularly in patients with toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Provide nutritional support early in the course of the disease either orally or via NG/NJ tube. Monitor weight regularly.
Good skin care involves avoiding trauma (i.e., adhesives, BP cuffs) using thin barriers or soft silicone tape instead when contact cannot be avoided.
All patients with Stevens–Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis should be managed at a tertiary care center or a burn center.
All patients with possible ocular involvement should have early involvement by an ophthalmologist.
Mortality is 1% to 3%.
If disease progresses to toxic epidermal necrolysis, mortality increases to 10% to 35%.

A retrospective cohort of 50 adult and 21 pediatric patients at a single institution found that of the adults, 31 had Stevens Johnson Syndrome (SJS), 17 had toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) and 2 had overlap. In adults, mortality was 6.5% for SJS and 35% for TEN. All 21 children had SJS, largely caused by mycoplasma pneumonia infection.
The SCORTEN score () predicts mortality in patients with Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
